title: Brijesh Kumar vs Vikas Gupta on 29 May, 2026
full_text: Brijesh Kumar vs Vikas Gupta on 29 May, 2026 IN THE COURT OF Ms. AASTHA SHARMA, LD. JMFC (N.I. Act)-03, SOUTH-EAST DISTRICT, SAKET COURTS COMPLEX: DELHI Brijesh Kumar Vs. Vikas Gupta CC No. 3531/2019 U/S 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 1. CNR number DLSE020106002019 2. Name of the complainant Sh. Brijesh Kumar, S/o Late Sh. Charan Singh, R/o H. No. B-26, Molarband Village, Badarpur, New Delhi- 110044. 3. Name of the accused person(s), parentage Sh. Vikas Gupta, & residential address S/o Sh. Jai Prakash Gupta, R/o B- 49/1, Molarband Village, Badarpur, New Delhi- 110044. Also At: AASTHA SHARMA H. No. 198, Ward No. 09, Shahuji Nagar, Milak Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA CC No. 3531/2019 Brijesh Kumar Vs. Vikas Gupta Page 1 of 15 Date: 2026.05.29 15:07:15 +0530 Rampur, UP. 4. Offence complained of or proved U/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 5. Plea of the accused Pleaded not guilty and claimed trial 6. Final Judgment/order Acquittal 7. Date of judgment/order 29.05.2026. Date of Institution : 22.03.2019. Date of Reserving Judgment/Order : 07.05.2026. Date of Pronouncement of Judgment/Order : 29.05.2026. ARGUING COUNSELS: Ld. Counsel for the complainant : Sh. Siddhanth Gautam Ld. Counsel for the Accused : Sh. Veer Pal Upadhyay JUDGMENT 1. Vide this judgment, this Court shall dispose of the present complaint filed by AASTHA the complainant Sh. Brijesh Kumar (hereinafter referred to as "complainant") against SHARMA Sh. Vikas Gupta under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 read Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA CC No. 3531/2019 Brijesh Kumar Vs. Vikas Gupta Page 2 of 15 Date: 2026.05.29 15:08:56 +0530 with Section 142 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as " NI Act "). Brief facts of the case: 2. It is the case of the complainant, A. That, the complainant runs a grocery store and accused was his neighbour and they had friendly relations with each other. That, in the first week of June 2016, the accused approached the complainant for a friendly loan of Rs. 5,00,000/- to meet some of his urgent requirement. That, the complainant had recently received consideration amount for a plot of land sold by him and therefore he advanced a sum of Rs. 5,00,000/- as friendly loan on June 12, 2016 and the accused promised to return the loan amount within 3 months. That, the complainant approached the accused to return the loan amount on multiple occasions and thereafter in discharge of his legal liability, the accused issued cheque bearing no. 030607 dated 18.01.2019 for loan amount of Rs. 5,00,000/- drawn on Oriental Bank of Commerce, MCIE Mathura Road, New Delhi and assured that the same will be honored on presentation. That, believing the assurances and representation of the accused, the complainant presented the abovesaid cheque with his banker Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank, Branch Meethapur Chowk, Jaitpur, New Delhi, however the said cheque was dishonoured with the remarks "Return Code/Reason-05" vide return memo dated 28.01.2019. B. In these circumstances, the complainant got issued a statutory legal demand notice to the accused through his counsel, dated 14.02.2019, thereby requiring the accused to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheques within a period of 15 days from the receipt of the said notice. The said notice under Sec. 138 of NI Act was sent to the AASTHA SHARMA accused through Registered AD/Speed Post/Courier at his correct address. That despite service of the above stated notice of demand, the Accused has deliberately Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA CC No. 3531/2019 Brijesh Kumar Vs. Vikas Gupta Page 3 of 15 Date: 2026.05.29 15:09:03 +0530 and willfully failed to comply with the said notice of demand and has failed to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheque within the stipulated period of 15 days from the date of receipt of the said notice. Consequently, this case was filed by the complainant against the accused, which was within the limitation period as laid down u/s 138 , NI Act. 3. In the pre-summoning evidence, the complainant examined himself on affidavit being Ex. CW1/X and relied on documents Ex. CW1/A to Ex. CW1/I. 4. Upon prima facie consideration of the pre-summoning evidence, the accused person was summoned. 5. Upon the appearance of the accused person, notice under Section 251 CrPC was served upon them to which he pleaded not guilty. The accused has admitted his signatures on the cheque in question and has stated that in 2012, he was in need of financial help for which he had approached the complainant and the complainant told him that he could arrange a loan of Rs. 50,000/- for him and for that, he had issued a cheque in question in favour of the complainant. The accused further stated that he never received the loan amount but also never asked for cheques back as he had good relations with the complainant. The accused has further denied receiving the legal demand notice. 6. CW-1 was examined-in-chief, cross-examined and discharged. Thereby, CE was closed on 29.04.2024. Accordingly, matter proceeded to the stage of recording the statement of the accused person. 7. Statement of accused person under Section 313 CrPC read with Section 281 AASTHA CrPC was recorded wherein the accused opted to lead defence evidence. However, SHARMA despite multiple opportunities being granted, the accused did not lead DE and therefore the right of the accused to lead DE was closed on 19.03.2026. Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA CC No. 3531/2019 Brijesh Kumar Vs. Vikas Gupta Page 4 of 15 Date: 2026.05.29 15:09:09 +0530 8. Thereafter, the matter was listed for final arguments. After hearing the final arguments from both sides, the matter was reserved for pronouncement of judgment. 9. It is well settled position of law that to constitute an offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled: I. drawing of the cheque by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, II. The cheque was issued for payment to another person for discharge in whole/part any debt or liability; III. Cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier. RBI in its notification DBOD.AML BC.No.47/14.01.001/2011-12 has reduced the aforesaid period from 6 months to 3 months. IV. Returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque; V. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid demanding payment of the cheque amount; VI. Failure of the drawer to make payment to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, of the amount covered by the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. AASTHA The offence under Section 138 , NI Act is made out against the drawer of the SHARMA cheque, only when all the aforementioned ingredients are fulfilled. Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA CC No. 3531/2019 Brijesh Kumar Vs. Vikas Gupta Page 5 of 15 Date: 2026.05.29 15:09:16 +0530 10. Analysing all the concerned provisions of law and various pronouncements in this regard, the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa [AIR 2019 SC 1983] held that: I. Once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the Act mandates that a presumption be drawn that the cheque in question was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. II. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. III. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. IV. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. It is therefore implied that the law regarding the presumption for the offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the presumptions under Section 118(a) and Section 139 have to be compulsorily raised as soon as the execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter the burden is shifted upon the accused to prove otherwise. Appreciation of evidence and marshalling of facts: AASTHA SHARMA Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA CC No. 3531/2019 Brijesh Kumar Vs. Vikas Gupta Page 6 of 15Date: 2026.05.29 15:09:24 +0530 11. Issuance of cheque: The complainant has filed on record the original cheque, i.e., bearing no. 030607 dated 18.01.2019 for Rs. 5,00,000/- drawn on Oriental Bank of Commerce, MCIE Mathura Road, New Delhi (Ex. CW1/A). In notice under Section 251 CrPC, the accused has admitted that the cheque in dispute belongs to him. It is also not disputed that the cheque in question is not drawn on the account maintained by the accused and it is impliedly admitted therefore that the accused is the drawer of the cheque. Therefore, ingredient number I stands fulfilled in the present case. 12. Presentment and dishonor of cheque: As per the RBI guidelines, it is essential for the cheque in question be to presented within a period of three months from the date on which they are drawn and the same be returned as unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque. In the case at hand, the cheque in question was returned vide return memo dated 28.01.2019 (Ex. CW1/C) due to the reason "Kindly Contact Drawer/Drawee Bank." By implication thereof, the cheque was presented within three months and the same was returned. Therefore, Ingredient number III & IV stand fulfilled in the present case. 13. Legal demand notice and payment by the accused thereof: The legal notice dated 14.02.2019 (Ex. CW1/D) was dispatched on 26.02.2019 vide Speed Post (Ex. CW1/F & Ex. CW1/G), i.e., within 30 days of return of the bank memo indicating cheques in question being unpaid. The fact that the legal demand notice has made a clear and unambiguous demand for payment of the cheque in question is not disputed. The accused has denied the receiving of legal demand notice in notice u/s 251 CrPC. However, as per the presumption raised under Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and Section 27 of General Clauses Act, if the legal demand AASTHA SHARMA notice is sent at the correct address, then the same shall be deemed to have been duly served, as per the precedent laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA CC No. 3531/2019 Brijesh Kumar Vs. Vikas Gupta Page 7 of 15 Date: 2026.05.29 15:09:31 +0530 Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed , (2007) 3 SCC (Cri). The ingredient number V is fulfilled by virtue of giving of legal demand notice within 30 days from the bank return memo. The receipt of legal demand notice by the accused is deemed to be admitted as per the discussion above. 14. Moving on, it is not disputed that the accused has not made the payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of the receipt of legal demand notice. Therefore, ingredient number VI also stands fulfilled in the present case. Presumption under Section 118A read with Section 139 , NI Act 15. The NI Act raises two presumptions in favour of the holder of the cheque, i.e., complainant; firstly, with regard to the issuance of cheque for consideration, as contained in Section 118(a) and secondly, with regard to the fact that the holder of cheque received the same for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, as contained in Section 139 of the Act. These presumptions shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability etc. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its judgment titled Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441 held that a reverse onus clause usually imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden and when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. It was further held that the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of AASTHA SHARMA his/her own. Once a probable defence is raised, then the onus is shifted to the complainant to establish that a legally enforceable liability existed in his favour and Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA CC No. 3531/2019 Brijesh Kumar Vs. Vikas Gupta Page 8 of 15 Date: 2026.05.29 15:09:37 +0530 the burden of proof on the complainant in this case is that of "beyond reasonable doubt." 16. The accused can rebut the presumption as raised under Section 138 , NI Act by: (a) putting forth his defence at the time of framing of notice u/s 251 CrPC; (b) cross-examining the complainant; (c) when statement of accused is recorded u/s 313 CrPC; (d) or by leading defence evidence, thereby demolishing the case of the complainant. Rebuttal of Presumption by Accused as to existence of legally enforceable debt 17. In light of the above discussion, since the accused has admitted to issuance of cheques, admitted the signatures on the cheques and legal notice has also been deemed to be served, what is left to be seen is whether the accused has been able to rebut the presumption against him, i.e., whether the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt? 18. In the present case, in order to discharge his initial burden to prove the abovementioned ingredients, the complainant relied upon the affidavit of the complainant being Ex. CW1/A and placed on record documents mentioned hereinbefore. The case of the complainant is that the accused had issued the cheque in question in discharge of his liability qua the loan taken from the complainant. The accused has been consistent in his defence and has stated that he needed financial help of Rs. 50,000/- in the year 2012 for which he approached the complainant and AASTHA SHARMA issued the cheque in question, however the accused never received the loan amount. Digitally signed by AASTHA CC No. 3531/2019 Brijesh Kumar Vs. Vikas Gupta Page 9 of 15 SHARMA Date: 2026.05.29 15:09:46 +0530 19. The accused in his cross-examination of the complainant has questioned the financial capacity of the complainant to extend the abovesaid loan. The complainant in his cross-examination dated 08.01.2024 has stated as follows: "...At the time when I advanced the loan to the accused, I used to earn Rs. 15,000/- to Rs. 16,000/- per month. There are four members in my family and there are expenses as well. Vol. I sold a plot of land and received money qua the same and advanced the loan to the accused..." "...I have given the total amount of Rs. 5,00,000/- in cash to the accused in one go. I cannot produce any documents showing that I have withdrawn the said amount from the bank. Vol. I can produce the documents of sale of my property if given opportunity.." The complainant later placed on record property documents, i.e., ikrarnama bay dated 28.05.2016 Ex. CW1/J (OSR) and agreement to sale dated 27.09.2016 Mark B by which the property was executed by the complainant in favour of one Ashwini Kumar. It is to be noted that the ikrarnama Ex. CW1/J (OSR) has stated that the amount of Rs. 1,75,000/- was transferred to the complainant on 28.05.2016 and the balance amount of Rs. 11,15,000/- shall be transferred by 08.08.2016. The complainant has himself in his complaint, evidence by way of affidavit and cross- examination as CW-1 has stated that he had advanced the abovesaid loan to the accused on 12.06.2016. A bare perusal of Ex. CW1/J (OSR) indicates that the complainant did not receive the consideration amount for the property from the buyer before 12.06.2016 to advance the abovesaid loan to the accused and therefore AASTHA the financial capacity of the complainant to advance the abovesaid loan remains SHARMA unproved. Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA CC No. 3531/2019 Brijesh Kumar Vs. Vikas Gupta Page 10 of 15 Date: 2026.05.29 15:09:56 +0530 20. Furthermore, the complainant in his cross-examination has himself admitted that no written loan agreement or any receipt was executed between the accused or complainant qua the loan in question. The complainant had further not shown the loan in question in ITR of the complainant. The complainant has admitted that his monthly earnings was Rs. 15,000/- to Rs. 16,000/- therefore not having the financial capacity to advance a sum of Rs. 5,00,000/- to the accused in one go. The complainant has also been unable to place any document on record to indicate withdrawal from his bank or possession of cash amount with him. The complainant has merely stated that he had received money from the buyer of his property in cash without any proof of the same. Further, the complainant has not even examined the buyer of his property to corroborate his claim. It is highly unlikely that the complainant, with meagre means shall advance a big sum of Rs. 5 lakhs without any documentary proof. At this stage, it would be relevant to refer to the decision of the Hon'ble High court of Delhi in the case titled as Sheela Sharma vs. Mahender Pal (2016 SCC Online Del 4696), where inter-alia, it was observed that: "31. In cases where the complainant claims to have advanced a friendly loan in cash, and where the transaction of loan is not evidenced by any other documentary or other reliable evidence, no doubt, the aspect whether the availability of funds in cash with the complainant/lender, and its advancement as loan to the accused have been reflected in Page no.14 of 17 Madan Khurana vs. Pankaj Sharma CC No. 2233-2016 the income tax returns of the complainant/lender, or not, become relevant. If, AASTHA the availability of funds, and the loan transaction itself is not so SHARMA reflected, that factor is taken note of by the Court as relevant to Digitally signed by AASTHA hold that the presumption under Section 118 and 139 of the NI SHARMA Date: 2026.05.29 15:10:25 +0530 CC No. 3531/2019 Brijesh Kumar Vs. Vikas Gupta Page 11 of 15 Act stands rebutted. However, these considerations would not be relevant, where loan transaction itself is otherwise established, either through documentary evidence-such as, a receipt or a loan agreement, or acknowledgement executed by the accused, or by oral evidence of an independent witness who is found to be credible. In the present case, the loan transaction, though not recorded in an agreement, or a receipt or acknowledgement executed by the accused, and though not reflected in the income-tax returns of the complainant, is evidenced by the oral testimony of CW-2, who is an independent witness and highly credible." Therefore, in cases in which the impugned loan transaction is in cash, the accused can raise a probable defence by questioning the financial capacity of the complainant, and once the said question is raised, the onus shifts on the complainant to prove his financial capacity. In the present case, admittedly, no documents were placed on record to show that the complainant was having sufficient funds with him to advance such a huge sum of money. Further, such a huge sum was provided by the complainant to the accused by taking out of his savings, as the consideration for the property was not received by the complainant till August 2016, and that too without obtaining any receipt or any other document in this regard, which cannot be equated with the conduct of a prudent man acting in similar circumstances. 21. In the instant case, the complainant has not only failed to bring any documentary evidence in support of his case to prove that the alleged amount of Rs. 5,00,000/- was advanced by him to the accused by bringing any documentary or oral evidence on record, there are several omissions and inconsistencies in his testimony as well, which indicates that the complainant's case does not stand on its own AASTHA SHARMA footing. The complainant has neither brought any documentary evidence to indicate Digitally signed by AASTHA CC No. 3531/2019 Brijesh Kumar Vs. Vikas Gupta Page 12 of 15 SHARMA Date: 2026.05.29 15:10:34 +0530 the loan advanced to the accused person, nor has he brought any other individual as complainant witness to corroborate his case. In view of the aforesaid findings and analysis, this court has arrived at an irresistible conclusion that the accused has been able to cast a shadow of reasonable doubt upon the case of the complainant by rebutting the mandatory presumption resting in its favour and by several inconsistencies in the version of the complainant. Once the accused had created a probable defence as to the legally enforceable liability, the onus shifted on the complainant to prove the existence of legally enforceable liability of the accused, as on the date of the drawal or presentation of the impugned cheques, which has not been fulfilled by the complainant in the present case. Since this basic ingredient which is pivotal to attract liability under Section 138 NI Act has not been proved by the complainant, accordingly, no offence of dishonour of the impugned cheque under the said Section is made out. 22. In light of the discussion above, ingredient no. II has not been fulfilled in the present case. Conclusion: 23. In view of the aforesaid discussion, the accused Vikas Gupta has been successful in establishing a probable defence on a standard of preponderance of probabilities to rebut the presumption under Section 118 and 139 of the NI Act by punching holes in the case of the complainant and making the case of the complainant doubtful. The accused has been successful in establishing a probable defence and as a consequence, questioning the existence of legally enforceable liability in favour of the complainant and that the cheque was not issued by accused in discharge of existing legally enforceable debt or liability owed to the complainant. AASTHA In the result of the analysis of the present case, the accused Vikas Gupta is hereby SHARMA Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA CC No. 3531/2019 Brijesh Kumar Vs. Vikas Gupta Page 13 of 15 Date: 2026.05.29 15:10:47 +0530 acquitted of the offence punishable under Section 138 , Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
